246.title: Don't guess (Avot 1:16)
246.hook: Gamaliel: find a teacher, free yourself of doubt, don't tithe by guesswork
246.carry: someone else's share was in the pile
246.howItsDone: Observant Jews in the land of Israel still separate tithes (ma'aser) from produce, and when a question of Jewish law comes up, many ask a rabbi rather than decide by guesswork.

segments.voice: Yesterday, say little: Shammai, and Abraham's morsel of bread that turned into a feast. Your line was just a morsel of bread. Day two hundred forty-six.

Dinner with six friends, one check. Somebody says, let's just call it about forty each. Nobody pulls out a calculator. Somewhere at the table, the person who only had soup is quietly paying for someone else's steak, and the one who had the steak is quietly relieved. Nobody meant any harm. It was just a guess. Today's sage worried about exactly that kind of guess, only his table was a farmer's harvest, and the people who went short were the poor.
screen: `ONE CHECK, SIX FRIENDS.` → `LET'S CALL IT FORTY EACH.` → `A HARVEST, AND THE POOR.`

segments.voice: The chain now reaches Rabban Gamaliel, called the Elder. Tradition says he was Hillel's grandson, and the Mishnah gives him the title Rabban, our master. His saying: make for yourself a teacher, remove yourself from doubt, and don't tithe by estimate too often. That last line needs a picture. In the land of Israel, parts of a farmer's harvest weren't his to keep. Some went to the priests, a tenth to the Levites, and in certain years a tenth to the poor. So a farmer stands in front of a heap of grain. He can measure it, or eyeball it and say, that's about a tenth. The commentators point out that a guess goes wrong both ways. Too little, and he keeps what belonged to someone else. Too much, and what he set aside isn't a proper tithe. Either way, he's living with doubt. Now the first two lines make sense. Make for yourself a teacher: Pirkei Avot already said this, back with Joshua ben Perachyah. Some commentators say that one was about learning, and this one is about decisions: when you don't know, ask someone who does, instead of making it up. And remove yourself from doubt: don't leave important things resting on a shrug. It's a small, practical saying that reaches a long way. Guessing feels easier than measuring. But when other people's share is in the pile, the easy guess costs somebody something.

segments.voice: Count each breath, in and out as one, and really count instead of estimating: one, two, three. If you lose track, don't round up; go back to one. It's harder than it sounds, and that's the point: attention is a kind of measuring.
Don't guess. Rabban Gamaliel's rule: find a teacher, step out of doubt, and measure what belongs to others instead of eyeballing it.
Your line: someone else's share was in the pile. A tenth is a number, not a feeling. Day two hundred forty-six, done.

247.title: Silence (Avot 1:17)
247.hook: Simeon: I found nothing better for a person than silence
247.howItsDone: Jewish tradition treats guarding speech (shemirat halashon) as a serious practice, and some Jews take on periods of deliberate silence, especially during times of reflection.

segments.voice: Yesterday, don't guess: Rabban Gamaliel and the farmer in front of the heap of grain. Your line was someone else's share was in the pile. Day two hundred forty-seven.
screen: `SOMEONE ELSE'S SHARE WAS IN THE PILE.`

segments.voice: The family dinner where everybody talks at once, every sentence louder than the one before, and nobody really listening. At the end of the table, one person says almost nothing, until, near the end, one quiet sentence that everybody remembers. Today's sage grew up in rooms like that: rooms full of sages, arguing over Torah. After a whole life among them, he reported that the best thing he found wasn't a speech.
screen: `EVERYONE TALKING AT ONCE.` → `ONE QUIET SENTENCE.` → `A LIFE AMONG THE SAGES.`

segments.voice: He's Simeon, the son of Rabban Gamaliel from yesterday, raised in the house of the leaders of the sages, surrounded by debate. His saying: all my days I grew up among the sages, and I found nothing better for a person than silence. The Hebrew says for the body, as if silence were good for you the way sleep is. Then two more lines. Study isn't the main thing; doing is. And whoever talks too much brings on sin. That last line sounds like an old proverb, and it is. Proverbs says something close: where words pile up, wrongdoing is never far away. Pile up enough words and something false, cruel or careless slips in. The Talmud puts a price tag on it: a word is worth one coin, silence is worth two. And much later in Pirkei Avot, Rabbi Akiva gives the line we're carrying today: a fence around wisdom is silence. Remember the fence around the Torah, from the start of the tractate? A fence doesn't hide what's inside. It protects it. Silence keeps what you know from spilling out carelessly, and leaves room for what you don't know yet to come in. This isn't a rule against speaking. Simeon's own teachers spent their lives talking about Torah. It's about the weight of words: fewer of them, chosen well, and followed by doing.

segments.voice: Two minutes of real silence: no words, not even in your head, if you can manage it. When a sentence starts forming, a reply, a plan, an argument, notice it and let it go unsaid. Listen instead, to the room, to your breath, to whatever's under the noise; you don't have to fill the quiet.
Silence. Shetikah in Hebrew. Simeon found nothing better for a person, and Rabbi Akiva called it a fence around wisdom.
Your line: silence is a fence. Not a wall, a fence, around what you know. Until tomorrow.

248.title: Truth, justice, peace (Avot 1:18)
248.hook: the world endures on three things: truth, justice and peace
248.carry: justice that makes peace in the gates
248.howItsDone: Jewish teaching treats truthfulness, fair judgment and peacemaking as linked duties, and the three are learned together from this saying, which closes the first chapter of Pirkei Avot.

segments.voice: Yesterday, silence: Simeon found nothing better, and Rabbi Akiva built a fence out of it. Your line was silence is a fence. Day two hundred forty-eight.

A three-legged stool sits steady even on an uneven floor, as long as all three legs are there. Take one away and it doesn't wobble. It falls. Chapter one of Pirkei Avot started, back with Simon the Just, by naming three things the world stands on: Torah, worship and kindness. Now, at the very end of the chapter, after the whole chain of teachers, another sage names three more. A second stool.
screen: `A THREE-LEGGED STOOL.` → `THREE PILLARS, AT THE START.` → `THREE MORE, AT THE END.`

segments.voice: The sage is Rabban Simeon ben Gamaliel, and his saying closes chapter one. The world endures on three things: on justice, on truth, and on peace. Then he gives a verse from the prophet Zechariah, who tells the people to judge with truth, and with a justice that makes peace, in their gates. All three in one line of scripture. Notice the difference from the start of the chapter. Simon the Just said what the world stands on, the reasons it exists at all. This saying is about what keeps it going day to day, in courts and markets and kitchens. One way to read it: the three hold each other up. Justice without truth is just power. Truth without peace can be a weapon. Peace without justice is only quiet. A teaching in the Jerusalem Talmud goes further: the three are really one thing, because when real justice is done, truth is done and peace is made. Now today's word. Truth, in Hebrew, is emet, spelled with three letters: alef, the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet, mem, near the middle, and tav, the very last. The rabbis noticed, and read it as truth that runs from beginning to end. And the Talmud calls truth God's own seal. That's a lot of weight on one small word. It's also a very ordinary one, the word Hebrew speakers use to say, really? Emet?

segments.voice: Think of something true you've been avoiding saying, to a friend, a partner, a boss, a parent: not a weapon or a lecture, just a true thing. Ask how it could come out with peace in it too, fair to them and gentle. Let the words get simpler and softer with each breath, without letting them stop being true.
Truth. Emet in Hebrew: spelled from the first letter of the alphabet to the last, and one of the three things the world endures on, with justice and peace.

249.title: Small ones count (Avot 2:1)
249.hook: Rabbi Judah: be as careful with a light commandment as a weighty one
249.carry: it will be well with you
249.howItsDone: Jewish practice gives attention to small commandments as well as great ones, and the command to send away the mother bird (shiluach haken) is often taught as the classic example of a 'light' mitzvah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, emet: the world endures on justice, truth and peace, the end of chapter one. Your line was justice that makes peace in the gates. Today, chapter two begins. Day two hundred forty-nine.
screen: `JUSTICE THAT MAKES PEACE IN THE GATES.`

segments.voice: You'd run into a burning building for your family. Obviously. But would you hold the door for the stranger with the stroller? Text back your aunt? Put the shopping cart back in the corral when it's raining? Most of us are ready for the big moments. It's the small ones we skip, because surely they don't count for much. Chapter two of Pirkei Avot opens with the man who put the whole Mishnah together, and one of the first things he teaches is about the small ones.
screen: `THE BURNING BUILDING.` → `THE SHOPPING CART IN THE RAIN.` → `THE MAN WHO GATHERED THE MISHNAH.`

segments.voice: He's Rabbi Judah the Prince, so respected that the Mishnah often just calls him Rabbi, as if there were only one. Around the year two hundred, he gathered generations of oral teaching into the Mishnah, the book Pirkei Avot is part of. His words: be as careful with a light commandment as with a weighty one, because you don't know the reward that's given for each. The Torah has hundreds of commandments, and it almost never tells you what each one is worth. The rabbis say that's on purpose. If you knew the price list, you'd only do the expensive ones. Their example is hard to forget. In Deuteronomy, if you find a bird's nest with the mother sitting on the eggs, you send the mother away before you take the eggs. It's one of the easiest commands in the Torah. It costs you nothing. And the Torah attaches to it the promise that it will be well with you, and you'll have long days. That's the same promise given for honoring your father and mother, one of the hardest commandments there is. The easiest and one of the hardest, the same reward. So don't sort your good deeds into ones that matter and ones that don't. Rabbi adds a kind of scale: weigh what a good deed costs you against what it brings, and what a wrong gains you against what it costs. Small things are on that scale too. And you never know which small one is the heavy one.

segments.voice: Let your day come to mind, and look for the tiniest good thing in it you usually skip: refilling the water jug, saying thank you to the driver, answering a message from someone lonely. Picture doing it with full attention, as if it were the most important thing you'll do today. Maybe it is; you don't know.
Rabbi Judah, who gathered the Mishnah and taught that a light commandment deserves the same care as a weighty one, since no one knows the reward of either.
Your line: it will be well with you. The mother bird and the parents, side by side. Day two hundred forty-nine.

250.title: An eye that sees (Avot 2:1)
250.hook: remember three things above you: an eye that sees, an ear that hears, a book that records
250.howItsDone: The saying is studied as a reminder that private conduct matters as much as public conduct, and that being seen includes the good as well as the bad.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rabbi Judah the Prince, the mother bird, and no price list for good deeds. Your line was it will be well with you. Today, the end of the same saying. Day two hundred fifty.

A police car slides into the rearview mirror, and suddenly the whole highway is driving the speed limit. There's a similar gap between the person someone is in public and the person they are alone at eleven at night with a phone. Today's saying is about that gap. It closes the teaching of Rabbi Judah the Prince we started yesterday: three things to keep in mind so you won't stumble. They're short enough for a sticky note on your fridge.
screen: `THE CAR IN THE MIRROR.` → `ALONE AT ELEVEN AT NIGHT.` → `THREE THINGS ON A STICKY NOTE.`

segments.voice: Here's how he ends. Look at three things and you won't come into the grip of sin. Know what is above you: an eye that sees, an ear that hears, and all your deeds written in a book. The first picture is being seen. The second is being heard, even the things you say under your breath, and that's the line we're carrying today. The third is being remembered: nothing you do simply vanishes. The prophet Malachi has a picture like this, a book of remembrance written before God for the people who revere God and think about God's name. Now, this could sound like a security camera, something to make you nervous. But it doesn't say an eye that punishes. It says an eye that sees. The same eye sees the kindness nobody else noticed, the ear hears the quiet apology, and the book records yesterday's small good deed too. Being seen can be a comfort as much as a warning. There's also a later reading, from Hasidic teachers, who played with the Hebrew words for know what is above you. They read them as know that what is above comes from you: what happens up there depends on what you do down here. Either way, the saying closes the gap between the public you and the eleven p.m. you. There's only one of you, and it's seen, heard, and remembered.
screen: `AN EYE, AN EAR, A BOOK.` · `SEEN, HEARD, REMEMBERED.` · `IT SEES THE GOOD TOO.` · `WHAT IS ABOVE COMES FROM YOU.` · then, large: `THE EAR HEARS.`

segments.voice: Imagine everything about this moment is noticed, not by a camera, but by someone who wishes you well: your posture, your breath, the worry you're carrying. Let yourself be seen that way, then think of one thing you'll do today when nobody's watching, and picture doing it as if someone were. If you pray, you can remember that, in this teaching, God sees and hears.
Malachi, the prophet who pictured a book of remembrance written before God, the same book Rabbi Judah's saying says your own deeds are written in.

251.title: Learning and labor (Avot 2:2)
251.hook: study joined with work is good; together they keep wrongdoing away
251.carry: two hands, each keeping the other steady
251.howItsDone: Some Jews combine a profession with regular Torah study, often a set time each day or week, while some communities support full-time study as a calling; both look to sayings like Avot 2:2.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Malachi's book of remembrance: an eye that sees, an ear that hears, and all your deeds written down. Your line was the ear hears.

There are two ways to get stuck. One person reads every book about changing their life and never changes a thing: all ideas, floating. Another works twelve-hour days, head down, and hasn't had a new thought in years: all motion, no meaning. Plenty of people lean one way or the other, depending on the season. Today's sage is the son of Rabbi Judah the Prince, the man who gathered the Mishnah. His saying: learning alone isn't enough.
screen: `ALL IDEAS, NO CHANGE.` → `ALL WORK, NO THOUGHT.` → `THE SON OF RABBI JUDAH.`

segments.voice: He's Rabban Gamaliel, and he opens with praise: beautiful is the study of Torah together with derekh eretz, because the effort of both keeps sin out of mind. Derekh eretz literally means the way of the land. Elsewhere it means good manners; here it means earning a living, a trade, the ordinary work of the world. Why would the two together keep wrongdoing away? One reading is simple: a mind busy with learning and hands busy with work don't leave much room for trouble. But there's more. Learning keeps work honest, because you bring what you've learned to the market and the workshop. Work keeps learning honest, because you have to live the ideas with real people and real money. Then the warning side: Torah study without work, Gamaliel says, ends in nothing and brings sin along with it. That's a strong line, and Jews have discussed the balance ever since. The Talmud records two sages who disagreed: one said plow and plant in season, and study too; the other worried that if people are always plowing, when will the Torah get learned? Today, some Jews combine a job with regular study, and some communities support people who study full-time as a sacred calling. Each side reads this saying closely. What they share is Gamaliel's picture: learning and labor aren't enemies. They're two hands, and each keeps the other steady.

segments.voice: Think of something you've learned recently, anywhere, even from one of these sayings; small ones count. Then think of the work waiting for you today, paid or unpaid: a meeting, a shift, a conversation with a customer or a child. Picture the idea showing up right there, the two meeting.
Derekh eretz. The way of the land, earning a living: paired with Torah study by Rabban Gamaliel, each keeping the other honest.

252.title: His will as yours (Avot 2:4)
252.hook: make God's will your will, so God makes your will His
252.howItsDone: Some Jewish teachers describe growth in observance as moving from doing a commandment because it is commanded to doing it with love, and this saying is studied as a picture of that change.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rabban Gamaliel paired Torah with derekh eretz, the work of the world. Your line was two hands, each keeping the other steady. Today, the same sage goes deeper.
screen: `TWO HANDS, EACH KEEPING THE OTHER STEADY.`

segments.voice: A kid cleans his room because he's told to. Years later, grown up, he cleans it because he actually likes a clean room. Same broom, same floor. But something changed inside: the rule stopped being someone else's and became his. That shift, from have to, to want to, is what today's saying is about. It's a bold line, and it talks about God's will and yours as if they could become the same thing.
screen: `TOLD TO CLEAN THE ROOM.` → `WANTING A CLEAN ROOM.` → `FROM HAVE TO, TO WANT TO.`

segments.voice: Rabban Gamaliel, son of Rabbi Judah, says this. Do His will as if it were your will, so that He will do your will as if it were His. Set aside your will before His will, so that He will set aside the will of others before yours. The Hebrew for will is ratzon: what you want, what pleases you, your desire. The saying is built like a mirror, your will and God's reflected back and forth. Commentators read it more than one way. Some take it practically: spend on doing good as gladly as you spend on what you want for yourself, and good things will come back to you. Others hear something inward. At first a commandment feels like someone else's rule. Over years of doing it, you can come to want it, the way the kid comes to want the clean room. Then what God wants and what you want aren't two different things anymore. The second half is harder. Sometimes what you want and what's good really do pull apart, and the saying asks you to let the good win. It doesn't promise you'll always get your way. It speaks of God setting aside the will of others, the pressure and plans of people around you, on your behalf. So the carry is simple: want what's good. And it closes a week of sayings: someone else's share was in the pile, silence, truth, justice and peace, it will be well with you, Malachi's book, two hands, each keeping the other steady, and today, his will as yours.
screen: `RATZON: WHAT YOU WANT.` · `A SAYING BUILT LIKE A MIRROR.` · `FROM HAVE TO, TO WANT TO.` · `SET YOUR WILL ASIDE.` · then, large: `WANT WHAT'S GOOD.`

segments.voice: Let one strong want come up, a thing, a result, someone's approval, and look at it honestly without pushing it away. Is there a good version inside it? Wanting money might hide wanting to care for someone; wanting to win might hide wanting to be seen. Let the wish lean toward that good thing, and if you pray, you can offer it to God.
Ratzon. Will, what you want: the word behind Rabban Gamaliel's mirror, do God's will as if it were your own.
Your line: want what's good. Have to can grow into want to. See you tomorrow.
